thig2.3:1.1: This verse is problematic and any translation is conjectural. I think that, like [thig1.11](), it hinges on double entendres of kitchen drudgery and sex. The nun here is presumably the mother of the Sumaṅgala at [thag1.43](), whose verses are similar.
thig2.3:1.2: The pestle (_musala_)  is the male, routinely paired with the female mortar (Śathapatha Brāhmaṇa 7.5.1.38).
thig2.3:1.3: If _vāpi_ is emended to _vāti_ (or _vāyi_), it refers to the wind that causes erections ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj1:10.17.6]()), cf. Rig Veda 1.28.6). Otherwise it is emphatic, “My husband was most certainly a mushroom”.
thig2.3:1.4: I prefer “mortar” for _ukkhalikā_ as the complement of “pestle”. Compare Sanskrit _ulūkhala_ (or _ulūkhalaka_) in the erotic hymn Rig Veda 1.28, and also ŚB 7.5.1.22, “the mortar is the womb of all breaths”. If the sense “little cauldron” is preferred, see ŚB 6.6.2.8, “the cauldron is female, the fire male” (also ŚB 7.1.1.42). The two terms are used in the same passage in this sense at ŚB 7.5.1.26. | _Deḍḍubha_ is a “water-snake” or eel ([pli-tv-kd15:29.2.2]()). But it is also a spelling of “drum”, as the mortar “speaks” when pounded like the “drum of victors” (RV 1.28.5). | For _vāti_ in the sense, “waft an odor”, see [vv38:6.3]().
